extracted.intended_audience: researchers in AI, computational humor, formal logic, and cognitive modeling of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Formalizing what makes a joke 'potentially funny' using belief revision and nonmonotonic reasoning: defining surprise, revelation, incongruity, measures of funniness, and constraints on teller/listener knowledge. Targets formal/computational models of jokes rather than informal comedy advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (Definition 4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement (α, β) is surprising for a listener associated with (K, ◦) if (K ◦ α) is consistent and (K ◦ α) ∧ (K ◦ (α ∧ β)) |= ⊥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise requires that the listener can form an expectation from the context (K ◦ α consistent) and that the revision by the punchline leads to a contradiction with that expectation. The definition excludes cases where the listener already knows α and β (they would be deducible from K). Example: models of K ◦ α and K ◦ (α ∧ β) are disjoint. Usual revision postulates ensure the first condition when α is consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing (Definition 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline β is revealing for (K, ◦) if (K ◦ β) is consistent and K ◦ β |= α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revelation means that once the punchline is known, the story's context α would be explained; the punchline plays the role of a revelation allowing resolution of cognitive dissonance. Consistency of K ◦ β is typically ensured by revision postulates when β is consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potentially funny (Definition 4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is potentially funny for a listener associated with (K, ◦) if it is surprising and its punchline is revealing for this listener.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both ingredients (surprise + revelation) must hold relative to the listener's epistemic state; funniness is listener-dependent because K and ◦ vary across listeners. The term 'potentially' reflects that not all listeners or tellers/situations will produce laughter even when formal conditions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listener capability: reasoning under incomplete information / defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding many jokes requires the listener's capability to reason under incomplete information (presence of defaults in Σ = (P, ∆)); listeners modeled with only strict rules (∆ empty) cannot be surprised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (psycho-rigidity) shows that if ∆ is empty, (α, β) is not potentially funny for the constructed listener. Thus a model of the listener should include defeasible/default knowledge to allow expectation formation and revision. This is a requirement on the epistemic state used to evaluate jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: listener already knows the joke / premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If α and β are already deducible from the listener's knowledge base K, the listener cannot be surprised and the joke fails to be funny in this sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal definitions explicitly exclude the possibility that the listener already knows the joke; ensure K does not entail α or β prior to presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline admissibility / consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline β should be admissible in that (K ◦ β) is consistent (ensured by revision postulates when β is consistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, a punchline that renders the listener's revised state inconsistent is not properly revealing; the formalism requires consistent K ◦ β to qualify as revealing/funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical punchlines: surprise vs revealing (note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsensical punchlines may create surprise but will not be revealing in the formal sense and thus typically will not satisfy the revealing requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote: nonsensical punchlines will not be revealing due to postulates (KM5) and (KM6). So while absurd/senseless lines can be surprising, they often fail the explanation/revelation condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative order: never give the punchline before the end (Proposition 4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (α, β) is potentially funny for a listener, then (β, α) is not potentially funny for that listener.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving the punchline early prevents the story from being surprising; use proper sequencing so revelation follows context. This formalizes the virtue of withholding the punchline until the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / minimal context (Proposition 4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding extraneous information α′ to the context (so using α ∧ α′) can make a previously potentially funny statement (α, β) no longer potentially funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer/more detailed contexts can destroy surprise or make the punchline insufficiently revealing. Examples show adding unrelated facts or the punchline itself as extra context can eliminate surprise or revelation. Keep context minimal and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / efficiency of the punchline (Definition 4.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement (α, β) is more efficient than (α, β′) if β is strictly more specific: β ≠ β′ and K ◦ β |= β′.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more precise/specific punchline is considered more efficient (concise) because it provides a tighter explanation. Efficiency is about minimality in terms of interpretations: prefer punchlines that entail other candidate punchlines under the revised state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascading jokes / multi-step revelations
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can be cascading sequences (ϕ1, ϕ2, ϕ3, ...) where surprising and revealing effects may occur at different steps (not necessarily simultaneous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A layered structure can produce intermediate laughs (e.g., an initial surprising remark followed by successive revelations). Formalization must account for multi-part narratives where different ϕi contribute to surprise and/or revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduality: measurable surprise and revealing levels (Definition 4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate quantitative levels to a statement (α, β): a surprise level (based on possibility/necessity measures from πΣ) and a revealing level N(α | K ◦ β) reflecting ineluctability of the revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures allow building a partial order on jokes addressed to the same listener, comparing potential funniness. The surprise level is computed relative to Π(α ∧ β) / N(α) as described; revealing level uses conditional necessity given K ◦ β. The paper notes additional gradual factors (effort, language, mood) that could be integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (Definition 5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement (α, β) is felt incongruous by a listener Σ = (P, ∆) with a norm ρ ∈ PN ∪ ∆N if (1) α ∧ β |∼m Σ\{ρ} Not ρ (violation of ρ) and (2) β |∼m Σ\{ρ} α (revelation in disregard of ρ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incongruity is modeled as the violation of a social norm ρ when reasoning while disregarding ρ; both the violation and the ability of β to reveal α under Σ without ρ are required. PN and ∆N are subsets of formulas considered norms. The definition handles norms represented both as integrity constraints P and as default rules ∆.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity as a special form of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity arises when a communication violates a fundamental communication principle or expresses an impossibility (e.g., carrying an elephant in a small car); it may be treated as an extreme form of incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absurdity often manifests when α is already inconsistent with P (P |= ¬α). In such cases the surprise notion from Section 4 may not apply; instead the revealing part can be considered by forgetting an obvious law (i.e., disregarding a norm). Examples: elephants in a car, impossible feats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard and limitations on considering a norm violated (Proposition 5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula ρ ∈ P such that P \ {ρ} |= ρ cannot be considered violated by a listener (P, ∆).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ρ is classically entailed by the rest of P, mere removal of ρ does not allow detecting its violation; this models listeners who are reluctant/unable to apprehend certain intended incongruities. Use careful selection of norms PN / ∆N when modeling incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting-as-if / ignoring a law to produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comic effects result from the teller 'acting as if' an obvious law or piece of knowledge does not apply, causing the listener to reason ignoring that law and perceive incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism explains examples where the revelation requires treating some rule as if it were absent (exceptional cases). The model formalizes this by considering Σ \ {ρ} in the incongruity definition; 'acting as if' is central to absurd and norm-violating humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-agent / teller considerations and social complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness depends not only on listener inference but also on teller choices: the teller should take into account what they know about the listener's norms, create complicity, and may exploit Gricean-like maxims or their violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes the need for multi-agent models to represent teller/listener interplay and superiority effects. Teller's style, timing, ability to create complicity, and anticipation of listener knowledge are important pragmatic criteria beyond formal surprise/revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other gradual contributors to funniness (nonformal factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional aspects contribute to the intensity of funniness: cognitive effort to understand, language level, comic effects of the narrator, mood of the listener, and the listener's capacity to inhibit emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are acknowledged as gradual and context-dependent; they can modulate or override formal surprise/revelation signals and are recommended topics for further research or integration into richer models.
